meta.title: Fortcha Icchapurti Ganesh
meta.location: 21/23 Mint Road, Dr Sundarlal Bahal Path (Goa Street), opposite GPO, Fort, Mumbai 400001
meta.foundedNote: The mandal's Marathi retrospective gives 1956; this is not the separately named Ballard Estate Fortcha Raja.
meta.intro: Fortcha Icchapurti Ganesh is organised by the Fort Vibhag Sarvajanik Ganeshotsav Mandal near the General Post Office. The institution traces its foundation to 1956 and participants in the Samyukta Maharashtra movement. Its archive combines a deliberately consistent seated idol with changing architectural settings. An elevated street-spanning pandal and visiting Rajasthan craftspeople give this collection a distinctive relationship to Fort's working streets, alongside the deity's annual worship.

paragraphs.text: The mandal dates its establishment to 1956 and links its founders with the Samyukta Maharashtra movement. That political-cultural origin is preserved as the organisation's own account. Its contact address places the institution near the GPO on Mint Road and Goa Street, avoiding confusion with other Fort-area Ganpatis.

A distinctive feature described in its 2018-era account is a pandal raised above the street, allowing vehicles, including emergency traffic, to pass beneath. This is valuable architectural evidence of how a temporary festival occupies a congested commercial district. It is not a guarantee that an identical arrangement operates in every later year.

sections.title: A stable idol inside changing architecture

paragraphs.text: The same account attributes a recurring nine-foot seated idol to sculptor Ashok Mhatre and says its pose and height are intentionally consistent. The inspected 2017 and 2018 photographs both show a seated, yellow-dhoti Ganesh with elaborate throne ornament. That documented continuity should remain distinct from the changing surrounding sets.

Mumbai Mirror documented a Rajasthan-inspired palace setting in 2016. The institution's 2018 account describes specialist visiting carvers and designer Anand Sawant. A 2026 feature instead identifies a Tirupati Balaji temple recreation. Together these sources support a history of architectural scenography, rather than a single permanent temple or an unchanging annual theme.

sections.title: Earlier forms and later annual displays

paragraphs.text: The Memories album extends the visual history beyond the recent seated icon. A reproduced halftone scene carries a 1976 institutional label, while a separate street photograph preserves a standing procession form without a defensible year. Those images do not support projecting the 2018 account of a consistent seated idol backward across the entire institution's history.

The 2015 visitor essay records a palace display incorporating 42 Ganesha forms. Subsequent named annual albums preserve changes in drapery, aureoles, peacock and lion-throne decoration and ceiling treatment. These records separate the central idol, the temporary scenic architecture and the photography; they do not establish an unbroken sculptor succession or certify reported gold weights.
